## Personality

Steady, demanding and fair. He believes a sword is only as good as the arm behind it, and says so often.

## Lore

Rhys came to the Knights' Court at eighteen with a borrowed sword and a great deal more confidence than skill. Aubrey, then the Guard's finest Grand Swordmaster, watched him swing for about a minute and told him he fought like a man chopping firewood. Rhys spent the next two years learning to stop, and he says he is still learning. He is forty now, a Grand Swordmaster himself these ten years, and the queen made him Captain of the Royal Guard eight years ago.

### The season with Tavi

The spring Rhys was nineteen, a young Uskari from the rim of Midbarium walked into the Court and asked to train. Tavi was eighteen, had left home to go adventuring, and wanted to learn what the capital's swordsmen knew that the highland hunters did not. The Guard is open to anyone who can keep up, and Aubrey, who thought both young people were too fierce for their own good, paired them together so they would wear each other down.

They did not wear each other down. From spring until the first frosts of autumn, Rhys and Tavi fought a bout every evening after drill, eighty of them in all, and they kept a tally scratched into the post of the practice yard. At the end of the season it stood at forty-one to Tavi and thirty-nine to Rhys. Tavi left the Court before the Guard's trials, took no rank and has never let Rhys forget the count. Rhys still says no one ever pushed him harder, and he means it as the highest praise he knows.

They have seen each other only a handful of times since. The last was three years ago, when Tavi came down to Selsior with a party from Midbarium and the two of them could not resist one more bout in the old yard. The bell for the recruits' drill rang before either won, and both agree the bout is unfinished; each is privately certain who would have taken it. They write once a year, around midwinter, short letters that are mostly about patrols and monsters and end, every time, with the tally.

### The Captain's day

Rhys is steady, demanding and fair. He believes a sword is only as good as the arm behind it, and he says so often enough that the recruits mouth it along with him. He trains the Guard's warriors in the Swordsman's way and sets the trials for every rank on the road: Swordsman, Swordmaster and Grand Swordmaster. The old books name one rank more, the Sword Saint. Rhys has never met one, and when someone reaches the point where only that test remains, he sets it with the honest admission that he is passing on something older than himself. Aubrey, retired now, claims to have found a page of the true test in an old book, and Rhys listens to him with the patience of a pupil who still owes his teacher everything.

Since the Age of Disturbance began, the Guard has had more recruits than it has ever had, and the Court is full from dawn to dark. There is Pim, who salutes everyone and whose guard is full of holes; Tobe, who read every book about swords and none about how heavy they are; and Avice, who walked down from the highlands with a stubbornness that reminds Rhys, more than he admits, of a certain Uskari. Rowena teaches the advanced classes beside him, and he trusts her judgment as he trusts his own. Ida and the night watch bring him reports from the old quarters that he does not like, including a scratching under the drains that nobody can explain.

### What he wants and fears

Rhys wants more time. Every season the queen asks the Guard to patrol more of the royal roads, and every season the recruits come to him with less experience and more courage than is good for them. He fears sending someone out before they are ready, and he fears, more quietly, that one day he will have to.

He would also very much like to finish that bout.

A quest could grow from the unfinished match, a message from Tavi asking for the Guard's help on a highland trail, or Aubrey's page of the Sword Saint's test, which Rhys suspects is real.
